name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q01 - Pathogens and their corresponding human diseases

questiontext.text:
Match the pathogens in Column I with the diseases they cause in Column II and select the correct combination.

Column I (Pathogen)Column II (Disease)
(A) Salmonella typhi(i) Amoebiasis
(B) Streptococcus pneumoniae(ii) Elephantiasis
(C) Entamoeba histolytica(iii) Typhoid
(D) Wuchereria bancrofti(iv) Pneumonia

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Infectious diseases in humans are caused by diverse groups of pathogens including bacteria, protozoans, and helminths, each targeting specific organs and producing characteristic symptoms.

Step 2: Individual Pathogen–Disease Evaluation
1. Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium that enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water and causes typhoid fever.
2. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterium that infects the alveoli of the lungs, causing them to fill with fluid and leading to pneumonia.
3. Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite residing in the human large intestine that causes amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery).
4. Wuchereria bancrofti is a filarial helminth worm that causes chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs, resulting in elephantiasis (filariasis).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are Salmonella typhi with typhoid, Streptococcus pneumoniae with pneumonia, Entamoeba histolytica with amoebiasis, and Wuchereria bancrofti with elephantiasis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q02 - Types of innate immunity barriers and examples

questiontext.text:
Match the types of innate immunity barriers with their corresponding examples and choose the correct option.

List I (Barrier Type)List II (Example)
(A) Physical barrier(i) Interferons
(B) Physiological barrier(ii) PMNL-neutrophils
(C) Cellular barrier(iii) Mucus coating of respiratory tract
(D) Cytokine barrier(iv) Acid in the stomach

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Innate immunity is a non-specific type of defence present at birth that operates through four distinct barrier categories to block or destroy foreign agents.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Barrier
1. Physical barriers prevent microbial entry into the body; examples include skin and the mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts.
2. Physiological barriers inhibit microbial growth through chemical secretions; examples include acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth, and tears from eyes.
3. Cellular barriers involve phagocytic and cytotoxic leukocytes that engulf and destroy microbes; examples include PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes, natural killer lymphocytes, and tissue macrophages.
4. Cytokine barriers consist of proteins called interferons secreted by virus-infected cells to protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matches pair physical barrier with mucus coating of respiratory tract, physiological barrier with acid in the stomach, cellular barrier with PMNL-neutrophils, and cytokine barrier with interferons.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q03 - Human diseases and their characteristic clinical features

questiontext.text:
Match the human diseases with their characteristic clinical or diagnostic features and select the correct option.

List I (Disease)List II (Characteristic Feature)
(A) Typhoid(i) Lips and fingernails turn gray to bluish in severe cases
(B) Pneumonia(ii) Dry, scaly lesions with intense itching
(C) Malaria(iii) Confirmed by Widal test
(D) Ringworm(iv) Recurring chill and high fever due to haemozoin

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each infectious disease presents distinct clinical manifestations and diagnostic markers depending on the affected tissue and pathogenic mechanism.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Disease
1. Typhoid causes sustained high fever (39° to 40°C), stomach pain, and intestinal perforation in severe cases, and is confirmed by the Widal test.
2. Pneumonia fills the lung alveoli with fluid, impairing respiration; in severe cases, lips and fingernails turn gray to bluish in colour.
3. Malaria involves rupture of RBCs by Plasmodium, releasing the toxic substance haemozoin, which causes recurring chill and high fever every three to four days.
4. Ringworm, caused by fungi (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton), produces dry, scaly lesions on skin, nails, and scalp accompanied by intense itching.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Typhoid pairs with confirmation by Widal test, pneumonia with gray-to-bluish lips and fingernails in severe cases, malaria with recurring chill and high fever due to haemozoin, and ringworm with dry, scaly lesions with intense itching.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q04 - Immunological terms and their functional descriptions

questiontext.text:
Match the immunological components or responses with their correct descriptions.

List IList II
(A) Colostrum(i) Responsible for graft rejection
(B) IgE(ii) Abundant IgA antibodies protecting the newborn infant
(C) Cell-mediated immunity(iii) Slow response upon host exposure to antigens
(D) Active immunity(iv) Antibodies produced in response to allergens

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Acquired immunity operates through humoral (antibody-mediated) and cell-mediated mechanisms, and can be acquired actively by antigen exposure or passively by receiving preformed antibodies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Colostrum is the yellowish fluid secreted by the mother during the initial days of lactation; it contains abundant IgA antibodies to provide passive immunity to the newborn infant.
2. IgE is the specific class of antibodies produced during an exaggerated immune response to environmental allergens.
3. Cell-mediated immunity (CMI), mediated by T-lymphocytes, differentiates 'self' from 'non-self' and is responsible for organ graft rejection.
4. Active immunity develops when a host is exposed to antigens and produces its own antibodies; this response is slow and takes time to give its full effective response.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The accurate pairings are colostrum with abundant IgA antibodies protecting the infant, IgE with antibodies produced against allergens, cell-mediated immunity with graft rejection, and active immunity with a slow response upon antigen exposure.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q05 - Human lymphoid organs and their characteristic features

questiontext.text:
Match the lymphoid organs or tissues with their characteristic features and select the correct option.

List I (Lymphoid Organ/Tissue)List II (Characteristic Feature)
(A) Bone marrow(i) Reduces to a very small size by puberty
(B) Thymus(ii) Constitutes about 50% of lymphoid tissue in human body
(C) Spleen(iii) Main lymphoid organ where all blood cells are produced
(D) MALT(iv) Large reservoir of erythrocytes and filter of blood

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human immune system comprises primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus) for lymphocyte origin and maturation, and secondary lymphoid organs/tissues (spleen, lymph nodes, MALT, etc.) for antigen interaction.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Organ/Tissue
1. Bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced.
2. Thymus is a lobed primary lymphoid organ near the heart that is quite large at birth but keeps reducing in size with age and becomes very small by puberty.
3. Spleen is a large bean-shaped organ that acts as a filter of the blood by trapping blood-borne microorganisms and serves as a large reservoir of erythrocytes.
4. MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lines the respiratory, digestive, and urogenital tracts and constitutes about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in the human body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Bone marrow pairs with production of all blood cells, thymus with reduction to a very small size by puberty, spleen with filtering blood and storing erythrocytes, and MALT with constituting about 50% of human lymphoid tissue.

questiontext.text:
Match the terms/techniques related to cancer with their correct descriptions.

List IList II
(A) Metastasis(i) Uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations
(B) Contact inhibition(ii) Property lost by cancerous cells
(C) Biopsy(iii) Histopathological study of thin stained tissue sections
(D) MRI(iv) Spread of tumor cells through blood to distant sites

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cancerous transformation involves loss of normal growth regulation and can be diagnosed through histopathological examination and non-invasive imaging methods.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Metastasis is the most feared property of malignant tumors, where cells sloughed from the primary tumor reach distant sites through blood and start new tumors.
2. Contact inhibition is the property by which normal cells stop uncontrolled division upon touching neighbouring cells; it is lost by cancerous cells.
3. Biopsy involves cutting a piece of suspected tissue into thin sections, staining it, and examining it under a microscope for histopathological studies.
4. MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to accurately detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings match metastasis with distant spread via blood, contact inhibition with the property lost by cancer cells, biopsy with histopathological study of stained tissue sections, and MRI with strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q07 - Abused drugs, plant sources, and physiological actions

questiontext.text:
Match the abused substances with their correct plant sources and physiological actions.

List I (Substance)List II (Source and Action)
(A) Heroin(i) Obtained from Erythroxylum coca; interferes with dopamine transport
(B) Cannabinoids(ii) Stimulates adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline
(C) Cocaine(iii) Obtained by acetylation of morphine; acts as a depressant
(D) Nicotine(iv) Obtained from Cannabis sativa; affects the cardiovascular system

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Commonly abused plant-derived drugs—opioids, cannabinoids, coca alkaloids, and tobacco alkaloids—interact with specific receptors or neurotransmitter/endocrine pathways in the human body.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Substance
1. Heroin (smack, chemically diacetylmorphine) is obtained by acetylation of morphine (from Papaver somniferum) and acts as a depressant that slows down body functions.
2. Cannabinoids are obtained from the inflorescences of Cannabis sativa and are known for their effects on the cardiovascular system of the body.
3. Cocaine (coca alkaloid) is obtained from Erythroxylum coca and interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine, producing euphoria and CNS stimulation.
4. Nicotine, an alkaloid in tobacco, stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline into the blood, raising blood pressure and heart rate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Heroin matches acetylation of morphine and depressant action, cannabinoids match Cannabis sativa and cardiovascular effects, cocaine matches Erythroxylum coca and interference with dopamine transport, and nicotine matches adrenal stimulation releasing adrenaline and nor-adrenaline.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q08 - Infectious diseases and their specific modes of transmission

questiontext.text:
Match the infectious diseases with their primary vectors, mechanical carriers, or modes of transmission.

List I (Disease)List II (Vector / Mode of Transmission)
(A) Amoebiasis(i) Aedes mosquito vector
(B) Filariasis(ii) Contaminated water, vegetables, and fruits with parasite eggs
(C) Dengue(iii) Houseflies acting as mechanical carriers contaminating food
(D) Ascariasis(iv) Bite of female mosquito vectors transmitting filarial worms

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Preventive public health measures depend on identifying whether a pathogen is transmitted via contaminated food and water, mechanical carriers, or specific biological insect vectors.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Disease
1. Amoebiasis (caused by Entamoeba histolytica) is transmitted primarily through faecal contamination of food and water, with houseflies acting as mechanical carriers from faeces to food.
2. Filariasis (caused by Wuchereria) is transmitted to a healthy person through the bite of female mosquito vectors.
3. Dengue (along with chikungunya) is a vector-borne viral disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
4. Ascariasis (caused by Ascaris) is acquired when a healthy person consumes water, vegetables, or fruits contaminated with parasite eggs excreted in infected faeces.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Amoebiasis pairs with houseflies as mechanical carriers, filariasis with female mosquito vectors carrying filarial worms, dengue with Aedes mosquitoes, and ascariasis with water, vegetables, and fruits contaminated with parasite eggs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_MATCH_Q09 - Clinical conditions, diagnostic tests, and physiological outcomes

questiontext.text:
Match the clinical terms or agents with their associated diagnostic role or physiological outcome.

List IList II
(A) ELISA(i) Widely used diagnostic test for AIDS
(B) Rheumatoid arthritis(ii) Masculinisation and abnormal menstrual cycles
(C) Histamine and serotonin(iii) Released from mast cells during allergic reactions
(D) Anabolic steroids in females(iv) Auto-immune disease where the body attacks self-cells

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Immune dysfunction can manifest as immunodeficiency (AIDS), hypersensitivity (allergy), or loss of self-tolerance (auto-immunity), while hormonal drug misuse causes endocrine side effects.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Item
1. ELISA (enzyme-linked immuno-sorbent assay) is a widely used diagnostic test for AIDS.
2. Rheumatoid arthritis is an auto-immune disease in which the body attacks its own self-cells.
3. Histamine and serotonin are inflammatory mediators released from mast cells that trigger the symptoms of allergic reactions.
4. Misuse of anabolic steroids in females causes side effects including masculinisation, abnormal menstrual cycles, excessive facial/body hair, enlargement of clitoris, and deepening of voice.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ELISA pairs with the diagnostic test for AIDS, rheumatoid arthritis with auto-immune disease attacking self-cells, histamine and serotonin with release from mast cells during allergy, and anabolic steroids in females with masculinisation and abnormal menstrual cycles.
